claims.text: Molecular Dynamics simulations can be used to study the thermal response of FeCuCrCoNi high-entropy-alloy nanoparticles as a function of particle size.
Molecular Dynamics can be combined with Monte Carlo exchange techniques to model high-entropy alloys.
MD and MC methods can capture atomistic thermal processes and finite-size effects in FeCuCrCoNi nanoparticles.
The initial FeCuCrCoNi nanoparticles are synthesized in a near-equilibrium state at room temperature.
The elements in the initial FeCuCrCoNi nanoparticles are randomly distributed.
Nanoparticle size can be systematically varied in MD simulations while applying controlled temperature ramps.
The simulations should span temperatures from room temperature to near the predicted melting point.
Periodic or free boundary conditions can be selected as appropriate for nanoparticle geometries.
The surface-to-volume ratio increases as nanoparticle size decreases.
An increased surface-to-volume ratio influences surface diffusion and atomic ordering.
Finite-size effects enhance the mobility of surface atoms.
Decreasing particle size alters the balance between bulk and surface energies.
Greater surface effects at smaller particle sizes reduce thermal stability.
Smaller FeCuCrCoNi nanoparticles will have lower effective melting temperatures or modified phase transitions.
Smaller nanoparticles are expected to exhibit earlier structural disorder than larger nanoparticles or bulk material under comparable heating conditions.
The validity of the simulations depends on interatomic potentials that capture multicomponent Fe-Cu-Cr-Co-Ni interactions.
The proposed interpretation is restricted primarily to near-spherical nanoparticles.
Morphological or compositional inhomogeneity may cause deviations from the predicted size dependence.
Current interatomic potentials may not accurately represent multicomponent HEA behavior at the nanoscale.
Absence of a systematic reduction in melting temperature or disorder-onset temperature with decreasing size would falsify the predicted size dependence.
